summary: This component fetches and displays comments from Bluesky (a social media platform) for a blog post. It converts the raw Bluesky data into React elements, handling text with special formatting like links, embedded images, and filtering out blocked users while preserving replies to those users. The component shows a loading state, handles errors gracefully, and displays a call-to-action if there are no comments yet.

explanations.16: This function takes a Bluesky post and converts its text into React elements, turning things like links (called 'facets') into actual clickable `<a>` tags in the output.
explanations.21: TextEncoder converts the plain text string into UTF-8 bytes (numbers 0-255), which is necessary because Bluesky's position markers (where links/formatting start and end) are measured in bytes, not character count — important for emoji and accented characters that take multiple bytes.
explanations.28: The forEach loop walks through each facet (like a link or mention) and builds an array of text parts, alternating between plain text and formatted elements like links.
explanations.32: This extracts the plain text between the last processed position and the current facet's start position, so we can include the regular text that comes before a link.
explanations.35: This searches the facet's features array to find if this particular facet is a link — facets can represent different things, so we check the `$type` field to identify what kind it is.
explanations.70: Instead of checking if `embed.$type === 'link'`, we use the `in` operator to check if the `external` property exists, because the TypeScript type doesn't narrow properly with literal equality checks (the catch-all type allows any `$type` string).
explanations.88: Similar to line 70, we check for the presence of an `images` property to determine if this is an image embed without relying on the `$type` field.
explanations.114: This extracts the post's unique ID from the end of its URI (the web address) by splitting on slashes and taking the last piece.
explanations.128: The padding increases with reply depth to create a visual indentation effect — replies at depth 0 have 1.5rem padding, depth 1 has 3rem, etc., showing the conversation hierarchy.
explanations.134: The `translate` function replaces `{name}` with the actual author's display name to create a personalized alt text for screen readers.
explanations.196: This state holds the flattened list of comments, initially null to indicate we haven't fetched yet (different from an empty array which means we fetched and found zero comments).
explanations.211: Promise.all runs both the API fetch and the blocked list fetch simultaneously, waiting for both to complete before continuing — this is faster than fetching them one after another.
explanations.214: If fetching the blocked list fails (network error, server down, etc.), we catch it and return an empty Set instead of crashing, so the component still works even if the moderation list is unavailable.
explanations.220: This creates a Set combining both hardcoded blocked handles and dynamically fetched ones, using Set for O(1) lookup speed when filtering comments.
explanations.225: This recursive function walks the nested reply tree (replies can have replies, which can have replies, etc.), adding each comment to the flat list along with its depth level for indentation.
explanations.231: We skip adding blocked users to the visible comments, but still recurse into their replies so legitimate responses to spam are still shown.
explanations.251: The dependency array ensures this effect runs only when the post key or config changes — if a user edits the page metadata, we re-fetch comments for the new post.
